**Prayut Chan-o-cha** ([Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"): ประยุทธ์ จันทร์โอชา, pronounced [[prā.jút tɕān.ʔōː.tɕʰāː]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Thai "Help:IPA/Thai") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Prayut_Chan-o-cha_Pronunciation.ogg "File:Prayut Chan-o-cha Pronunciation.ogg"); born 21 March 1954) is a Thai former politician and military officer who became the 29th [prime minister of Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_minister_of_Thailand "Prime minister of Thailand") after seizing power in the [2014 coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Thai_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2014 Thai coup d'état") and served until 2023. He was concurrently the [minister of defence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_defence_ministers_of_Thailand "List of defence ministers of Thailand") in his own government from 2019 to 2023.[[2]](#cite_note-5) Prayut served as [commander-in-chief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander-in-Chief_of_the_Royal_Thai_Army "Commander-in-Chief of the Royal Thai Army") of the [Royal Thai Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Thai_Army "Royal Thai Army") from 2010 to 2014[[3]](#cite_note-6)[[4]](#cite_note-7) and led the coup d'état which installed the [National Council for Peace and Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_for_Peace_and_Order "National Council for Peace and Order") (NCPO), the [military junta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_junta "Military junta") which governed Thailand between 22 May 2014 and 10 July 2019.[[5]](#cite_note-8)

After his appointment as army chief in 2010, Prayut was characterised as a [royalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royalist "Royalist") and an opponent of former prime minister [Thaksin Shinawatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thaksin_Shinawatra "Thaksin Shinawatra").[[6]](#cite_note-9) Considered a hardliner within the military, he was one of the leading proponents of military crackdowns on the [Red Shirt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Shirts_(Thailand) "Red Shirts (Thailand)") demonstrations of [April 2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Thai_political_unrest "2009 Thai political unrest") and [April–May 2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Thai_political_protests "2010 Thai political protests").[[7]](#cite_note-10)[[8]](#cite_note-11) He later sought to moderate his profile, talking to relatives of protesters who were killed in the bloody conflict[[9]](#cite_note-12) and cooperating with the government of [Yingluck Shinawatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yingluck_Shinawatra "Yingluck Shinawatra"),[[10]](#cite_note-13) who won [parliamentary elections in July 2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Thai_general_election "2011 Thai general election").

During the [political crisis that began in November 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013%E2%80%932014_Thai_political_crisis "2013–2014 Thai political crisis") and involved protests against the [caretaker government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yingluck_cabinet "Yingluck cabinet") of Yingluck, Prayut claimed that the army was neutral[[11]](#cite_note-14) and would not launch a coup. However, in May 2014, Prayut launched a military coup against the government and assumed control of the country as dictator and leader of the NCPO.[[12]](#cite_note-npkc-15) He later issued an [interim constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_interim_constitution_of_Thailand "2014 interim constitution of Thailand"), granting himself sweeping powers and giving himself amnesty for staging the coup.[[13]](#cite_note-16) In August 2014, an unelected military-dominated [national legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Thailand "National Assembly of Thailand") appointed him Prime Minister of Thailand.[[14]](#cite_note-17)[[15]](#cite_note-ThailandPM-18)

Prayut led an [authoritarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarian "Authoritarian") regime in Thailand.[[16]](#cite_note-dcttr-19) After seizing power, Prayut's government oversaw a significant crackdown on dissent.[[17]](#cite_note-dissent-20) He formulated "twelve values" based on traditional Thai values and suggested that these be included in school lessons.[[18]](#cite_note-21)[[19]](#cite_note-erased-22)[[20]](#cite_note-12_values-23) Measures were implemented to limit public discussions about democracy and criticism of the government, including increases in Internet and media censorship.[[21]](#cite_note-discussion-24) Prayut was elected as prime minister following the disputed [2019 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Thai_general_election "2019 Thai general election"), after having ruled as an unelected [strongman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_strongman "Political strongman") since 2014.[[22]](#cite_note-25) Following the results for [United Thai Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Thai_Nation_Party "United Thai Nation Party") which finished third in the [2023 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Thai_general_election "2023 Thai general election"), Prayut announced his retirement from politics, serving in a caretaker position until the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(Thailand) "National Assembly (Thailand)") voted for a new prime minister on 22 August.[[23]](#cite_note-26)[[24]](#cite_note-27) He was succeeded by [Srettha Thavisin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srettha_Thavisin "Srettha Thavisin") of the [Pheu Thai party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheu_Thai_Party "Pheu Thai Party"), after nine years in power.

After his political retirement, Prayut was appointed a [Privy Councilor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_Thailand "Privy Council of Thailand") on 29 November in the same year.[[25]](#cite_note-BP-PrivyCouncil-28)

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prayut_Chan-o-cha&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Born to an army Colonel, Prapat Chan-o-cha, native from Bangkok, and a school teacher, Khemphet Chan-o-cha, native from [Chaiyaphum province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaiyaphum_province "Chaiyaphum province"), he was the eldest child of four siblings.[[26]](#cite_note-29) He studied at Sahakit School in [Lopburi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lopburi "Lopburi") (now known as Lopburi Technical college), where his mother taught. For junior highschool, he spent only a year at Phibulwitthayalai Lopburi School because his father, an army officer, moved often. Then at the grade 8, he moved to Wat Nuannoradit School in [Phasi Charoen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phasi_Charoen_district "Phasi Charoen district"), where he was selected as one of the best students in a student magazine.[[27]](#cite_note-30)

In 1971, Prayut spent his senior highschool year at the [Armed Forces Academies Preparatory School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_Academies_Preparatory_School "Armed Forces Academies Preparatory School") (AFAPS) Class 12, and in 1976, became a cadet at [Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chulachomklao_Royal_Military_Academy "Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy") Class 23. He graduated with a bachelor of science degree. While in the academy, he finished Infantry Officer Basic Course Class 51 in his first year and Infantry Officer Advanced Course, Class 34 in 1981. Before starting his military career, he graduated from Command and General Staff College (CGSC) Class 63 in 1985.[[28]](#cite_note-ocha1-31)

### Queen's Guards (1986–2010)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prayut_Chan-o-cha&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Queen's Guards (1986–2010)")]

After graduating from the [Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chulachomklao_Royal_Military_Academy "Chulachomklao Royal Military Academy"), Prayut started his career as a [Major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_ranks_of_the_Thai_armed_forces "Military ranks of the Thai armed forces"). He was a royal guard under Prime Minister [Prem Tinsulanonda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prem_Tinsulanonda "Prem Tinsulanonda") in 1987.[[29]](#cite_note-32) Three years later, Prayut served in the [21st Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_Infantry_Regiment_(Thailand) "21st Infantry Regiment (Thailand)"), which is granted [Royal Guard status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Guards_(Thailand)#Notable_units "Royal Guards (Thailand)") as the Queen's Guards ([Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"): ทหารเสือราชินี, lit. 'Queen's Musketeer'). In 2001, he served as a deputy commanding general in the [2nd Infantry Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_Infantry_Division_(Thailand) "2nd Infantry Division (Thailand)"), becoming its commanding general one year later. In 2005, he became a deputy commanding general of the 1st Army, which included the 2nd Infantry Division. He was seen as one of the leaders of the alliance behind the [2006 Thai coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Thai_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2006 Thai coup d'état").[[30]](#cite_note-thitinan-33)

Like his direct predecessor, [Anupong Paochinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupong_Paochinda "Anupong Paochinda"), and former defence minister [Prawit Wongsuwon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prawit_Wongsuwon "Prawit Wongsuwon"), Prayut is a member of the army's "eastern tigers" faction. Most of them, like Prayut, began their military careers in the 2nd Infantry Division, headquartered in eastern Thailand, particularly in the [21st Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_Infantry_Regiment_(Thailand) "21st Infantry Regiment (Thailand)") (Queen's Guards).[[31]](#cite_note-34)[[32]](#cite_note-35)[[33]](#cite_note-36)[[34]](#cite_note-37)

After the 2006 coup, Prayut was appointed to the [National Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Legislative_Assembly_of_Thailand_(2006) "National Legislative Assembly of Thailand (2006)"). In this capacity, he joined the Committee on Environment and Natural Resources. Prayut sits on the executive boards of a number of companies including a state electricity utility company, the [Metropolitan Electricity Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Electricity_Authority "Metropolitan Electricity Authority") (MEA). From 2007 to 2010 he was independent director at [Thai Oil Public Co, Ltd.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_Oil "Thai Oil") Since 7 October 2010 he has been a director of [Thai Military Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TMB_Bank "TMB Bank")[[28]](#cite_note-ocha1-31) and chairman of the [Army United Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_United_F.C. "Army United F.C."). Prayut attended management course in the [National Defence College of Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Defence_College_of_Thailand "National Defence College of Thailand") (NDC) Class 20, in 2007. He was the chief of staff of the Royal Thai Army from 2008 to 2009, and in 2009 he was appointed honorary adjutant to the king.

### Army chief (2010–2014)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Prayut_Chan-o-cha&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Army chief (2010–2014)")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/General_Prayuth_Chan-ocha.jpg/250px-General_Prayuth_Chan-ocha.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:General_Prayuth_Chan-ocha.jpg)

General Prayuth in 2010

In 2010, he succeeded [Anupong Paochinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupong_Paochinda "Anupong Paochinda") as commander in chief.[[28]](#cite_note-ocha1-31)[[35]](#cite_note-38) On taking over, Prayut had stated that his mandates would be to maintain Thailand's sovereignty and to protect the [monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Thailand "Monarchy of Thailand"). His uncommon promotion was seen as a revealing of the influence of the Queen's Guards.[[30]](#cite_note-thitinan-33)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Prayut_Chan-O-Cha_in_1st_Infantry_Regiment%27s_royal_guard_uniform.jpg/250px-Prayut_Chan-O-Cha_in_1st_Infantry_Regiment%27s_royal_guard_uniform.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prayut_Chan-O-Cha_in_1st_Infantry_Regiment's_royal_guard_uniform.jpg)

Prayut in Royal Guards uniform, 2011

Amid the [2010 Thai political protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Thai_political_protests "2010 Thai political protests"), Prayut was the part of executive of the [Centre for the Resolution of Emergency Situations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_the_Resolution_of_Emergency_Situations?action=edit&redlink=1 "Centre for the Resolution of Emergency Situations (page does not exist)") (CRES), a special government agency that was found by Prime Minister [Abhisit Vejjajiva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abhisit_Vejjajiva "Abhisit Vejjajiva") and Deputy-Prime Minister [Suthep Thaugsuban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suthep_Thaugsuban "Suthep Thaugsuban"). Queen's Guards army general, [Anupong Paochinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anupong_Paochinda "Anupong Paochinda") was the leader of the violent [2010 Thai military crackdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Thai_military_crackdown "2010 Thai military crackdown") before Prayut stepped up to replace Anupong. Thitinan Pongsudhirak, a visiting scholar at [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University")'s Centre on Democracy, commented that Prayut was seen as more hardline than Anupong, and in April 2009, during the [red shirts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Shirts_(Thailand) "Red Shirts (Thailand)")' uprising, Anupong was nominally in charge but Prayut appeared to be directing the dispersing the red shirt protesters.[[36]](#cite_note-39)

Prayut had led the CRES from 5 October to 21 December 2010, in which he used authoritarian methods to control a political situation. The CRES banned symbolic political-dividing products such as Prime Minister Abhisit face on a sandal.[[37]](#cite_note-40)[[38]](#cite_note-41) After the CRES dissolved, in 2011, Prayut became part of the opposition to [Yingluck Shinawatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yingluck_Shinawatra "Yingluck Shinawatra")'s [Pheu Thai Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheu_Thai_Party "Pheu Thai Party") in the [2011 Thai general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Thai_general_election "2011 Thai general election"). He told the media that he stood in the middle, but urged Thai people not to vote for Pheu Thai, saying it would lead to "chaos and violence".[[39]](#cite_note-42) He intended to stop a violation of [monarchy defamation law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A8se-majest%C3%A9_in_Thailand "Lèse-majesté in Thailand") by [red shirts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Shirts_(Thailand) "Red Shirts (Thailand)") activists who support Yingluck. He vowed to sacrifice his life to protect the monarchy.[[40]](#cite_note-43) Before the election date, he urged the people to vote for the party that would protect the monarchy.[[41]](#cite_note-44) Eventually, Pheu Thai Party won the election in a landslide. [Pavin Chachavalpongpun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavin_Chachavalpongpun "Pavin Chachavalpongpun") called on Yingluck to sack Prayut, in order to remind the military to stay out of politics.[[42]](#cite_note-45)

In the late 2011, Prayut heavily criticised the [Nitirat group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitirat_Group "Nitirat Group"), led by [Worachet Pakeerut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worachet_Pakeerut "Worachet Pakeerut") and [Piyabutr Saengkanokkul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piyabutr_Saengkanokkul "Piyabutr Saengkanokkul"), who campaigned for constitutional reform and a change of Thailand's [lèse majesté law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A8se_majest%C3%A9_in_Thailand "Lèse majesté in Thailand"). Prayut warned them that they would violate the rule of law in Thailand.[[43]](#cite_note-46)

General elections were held in [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand") on 14 May 2023 to elect 500 members of the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_(Thailand) "House of Representatives (Thailand)").[[2]](#cite_note-3) The [Move Forward Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Move_Forward_Party "Move Forward Party"), led by [Pita Limjaroenrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pita_Limjaroenrat "Pita Limjaroenrat"), surprised analysts by winning the most seats, followed by fellow opposition party [Pheu Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheu_Thai_Party "Pheu Thai Party") who had won the most seats in the [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Thai_general_election "2011 Thai general election") and [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Thai_general_election "2019 Thai general election") elections. Turnout was a record 75.22%.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-4)[[4]](#cite_note-5)

The elections were held using a [parallel voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_voting "Parallel voting") system as in the [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_constitution_of_Thailand "1997 constitution of Thailand") and [2007 constitutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_constitution_of_Thailand "2007 constitution of Thailand"), in contrast to the [mixed-member apportionment system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-member_proportional_representation "Mixed-member proportional representation") used in 2019. Like in 2019, the elected prime minister did not need to be a member of the House and would be chosen by the full [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(Thailand) "National Assembly (Thailand)"), including the 250 military-appointed members of the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Thailand "Senate of Thailand"), for a total 376-seat majority. Due to the structure of the National Assembly, experts had warned of a possible [gridlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gridlock_(politics) "Gridlock (politics)") scenario in which the current opposition parties secure more than half of the House votes but are obstructed in the Senate. Additionally, the Election Commission had received criticism over untrustworthiness, unprofessionalism, and bias in its conducting of the voting process.

Sixty-seven parties vied for seats. The ruling conservative [coalition government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_government "Coalition government") was composed of the major [Palang Pracharath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palang_Pracharath_Party "Palang Pracharath Party"), [Bhumjai Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhumjai_Thai_Party "Bhumjai Thai Party"), and [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democrat_Party_(Thailand) "Democrat Party (Thailand)") parties, and smaller parties including the new [United Thai Nation Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Thai_Nation_Party "United Thai Nation Party"), who nominated former junta leader and incumbent prime minister [Prayut Chan-o-cha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prayut_Chan-o-cha "Prayut Chan-o-cha") after his split with Palang Pracharath. The pro-democratic opposition was led by the Pheu Thai and Move Forward parties, the latter being the effective successor of the dissolved [Future Forward Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_Forward_Party "Future Forward Party"), which had performed unexpectedly well in the [2019 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Thai_general_election "2019 Thai general election"). Political campaigns focused on the [Thai economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_economy "Thai economy"), especially its recovery from the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Thailand "COVID-19 pandemic in Thailand"). Some parties, most notably Move Forward, also highlighted [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressivism "Progressivism") issues,[[5]](#cite_note-6) and challenged long-held social norms in Thailand.

Pita's Move Forward initially formed a coalition with the other pro-democracy, anti-military parties, which had a majority in the lower house but was unable to form a government after being functionally blocked by allies of the monarchy and military in the Senate. Pheu Thai then assumed the lead, dissolving its alliance with Move Forward and allying instead with conservative, pro-military parties. It then nominated real estate tycoon [Srettha Thavisin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srettha_Thavisin "Srettha Thavisin") as prime minister. He was elected by Parliament on 22 August.[[6]](#cite_note-7)

On August 7, 2024, Thailand's [Constitutional Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Thailand "Constitutional Court of Thailand") banned the victors of the election, the Move Forward Party and all of its leaders from politics for its proposal to reform the [lèse-majesté law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A8se-majest%C3%A9_in_Thailand "Lèse-majesté in Thailand"), arguing it posed a threat to the constitutional order.[[7]](#cite_note-Economist1-8)

Following a [political crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013%E2%80%932014_Thai_political_crisis "2013–2014 Thai political crisis") in [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), the military staged [a coup d'état in 2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Thai_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2014 Thai coup d'état"), ousting [the civilian caretaker government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yingluck_cabinet "Yingluck cabinet") of [Yingluck Shinawatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yingluck_Shinawatra "Yingluck Shinawatra"). The military junta, known as the [National Council for Peace and Order (NCPO)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_for_Peace_and_Order "National Council for Peace and Order"), rose to power under the leadership of former army chief [Prayut Chan-o-cha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prayut_Chan-o-cha "Prayut Chan-o-cha") as [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Thailand "Prime Minister of Thailand"). In 2016, the NCPO completed the drafting of [a new constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_constitution_of_Thailand "2017 constitution of Thailand") and held [a referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Thai_constitutional_referendum "2016 Thai constitutional referendum") to approve it. They banned criticism of the draft constitution and prohibited monitoring of the referendum. Activists against the document were arrested, detained, and prosecuted in military courts,[[8]](#cite_note-9) whilst voters who expressed their intention to vote against the draft were also arrested and prosecuted by the military regime.[[9]](#cite_note-10)

In 2019, after numerous delays, the junta finally held [a general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Thai_general_election "2019 Thai general election") on 24 March. The elections were seen as a skewed race in which Prayut had an unfair advantage, with the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Thailand "Senate of Thailand") wholly appointed by the junta and the constituencies redrawn last-minute.[[10]](#cite_note-11)[[11]](#cite_note-12) After the election, the pro-junta [Palang Pracharath party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palang_Pracharath_Party "Palang Pracharath Party") formed a [coalition government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_government "Coalition government"), with Prayut selected by the parliament for another term as prime minister even though his party did not win the most seats.[[12]](#cite_note-WSJ-13)

Prayut began his second term as prime minister on 9 June 2019.[[13]](#cite_note-14) According to the current constitution, a prime minister can only serve for a maximum of eight years. However, the end of Prayut's term as the prime minister of Thailand is disputed since there are many interpretations about the beginning of his term.[[14]](#cite_note-:0-15)[[15]](#cite_note-16)[[16]](#cite_note-17) On 30 September 2022, the [Constitutional Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Thailand "Constitutional Court of Thailand") finally ruled that Prayut's term began in 2017 along with the new constitution, meaning that he may serve as the prime minister until 2025, if he is selected by the parliament again.

The [2020–2021 nationwide protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%932021_Thai_protests "2020–2021 Thai protests") started as demonstrations against the premiership of Prayuth but later expanded to include numerous long-overlooked issues in Thai society, and unprecedented demands to reform the monarchy. The Thai royal family is protected by [a lèse-majesté law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A8se-majest%C3%A9_in_Thailand "Lèse-majesté in Thailand"). Even though the protests largely died down due to crackdown, repression, and COVID-19 restrictions, it was anticipated that activism could resurge in this election and afterwards.[[17]](#cite_note-18)

The end of 2022 saw the split in the ruling Palang Pracharath Party between Prayut and his close associate [Prawit Wongsuwon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prawit_Wongsuwon "Prawit Wongsuwon"), after the latter showed accommodation towards the main opposition [Pheu Thai Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheu_Thai_Party "Pheu Thai Party"). Prayut was expected to join the new [United Thai Nation Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Thai_Nation_Party "United Thai Nation Party") along with his loyalists in the Palang Pracharath Party.[[18]](#cite_note-19) Forty politicians, including 34 incumbent MPs from both coalition and opposition camps, also resigned from their parties to join [Bhumjai Thai Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhumjai_Thai_Party "Bhumjai Thai Party") to increase their winning chances in this election.[[19]](#cite_note-20) On 23 December 2022, Prayut announced his intention to apply for membership of the United Thai Nation Party, as well as becoming the party's sole prime ministerial candidate.[[20]](#cite_note-21)

Rumor of a possible coup was circulated long before the election. In September 2022, a cabinet minister, [Chaiwut Thanakamanusorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaiwut_Thanakamanusorn "Chaiwut Thanakamanusorn"), warned that protesting may result in the cancellation of the election.[[21]](#cite_note-22)

Unlike the preceding [2019 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Thai_general_election "2019 Thai general election"), which used a form of [mixed-member proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-member_proportional_representation "Mixed-member proportional representation") with 350 constituency seats and the remaining 150 being [levelling seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levelling_seat "Levelling seat"), the electoral system was changed in a 2021 amendment of the constitution which restored the pre-2017 [parallel voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_voting "Parallel voting") system and removed the [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation "Proportional representation") mechanism.

Of the 500 members of the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_(Thailand) "House of Representatives (Thailand)") to be elected, 400 seats were elected from single-member constituencies by [first-past-the-post voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-past-the-post_voting "First-past-the-post voting") (an increase of 50), and 100 party-list seats—filled separately and no longer serving as leveling seats—are voted on in a separate ballot (unlike in the 2019 election, where only one vote was cast by each voter to determine both constituency and levelling seats).[[22]](#cite_note-23) The change was criticised by smaller parties as the system benefits larger parties—especially the ruling Palang Pracharath Party and the main opposition party Pheu Thai, who both supported the amendment—at the expense of smaller ones, including the progressive [Move Forward Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Move_Forward_Party "Move Forward Party"), whose predecessor [Future Forward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_Forward_Party "Future Forward Party") performed successfully in 2019 thanks to the proportional representation system.[[23]](#cite_note-24)

### Prime ministerial candidates

Parliament's vote for prime minister will take place in a joint session with the 250-seat [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Thailand "Senate of Thailand") appointed by the junta, according to the constitution's provisional terms. In 2019, all the senators unanimously voted for then-junta leader Prayut.[[25]](#cite_note-26) As the term of the NCPO-appointed Senate lasts until 2024, it is expected to exert influence into this election as well.[[26]](#cite_note-27)

Due to this rule, the anti-junta camp had to secure at least 376 votes in order to select their candidates,[[12]](#cite_note-WSJ-13) while a simple majority in the House could still result in a candidate from the pro-junta coalition winning the selection. If no candidates secured at least 376 votes in the Parliament, it could lead to a deadlock[[27]](#cite_note-28) and pave the way for a person not in the parties' list of candidates becoming prime minister as written in the Constitution. Such a scenario led some to call for [strategic voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_voting "Strategic voting") for larger anti-junta parties most likely to win in each constituency.

In January 2023, two youth political activists began a hunger strike calling for the release of political prisoners detained before trial. Many of them were charged with lèse-majesté, which led to another debate on amending or cancellation of the law. Political parties were asked for their stance on the issue.[[33]](#cite_note-34)

Beginning in January 2023, many civil society organizations called for volunteers to keep their eyes on the election process, citing the untrustworthiness of the Election Commission and its decision not to report the election result in real-time.[[34]](#cite_note-35) As of March 2023, the movement had grown to 50 organizations, including media, who declared they would report the unofficial election result when the commission would not.[[35]](#cite_note-36)

On 20 March 2023, the House of Representatives was dissolved—three days before the term ended. Due to a legal technicality, the election date was postponed for another week from 7 May 2023. The move also allowed politicians more time to switch parties, which many analysts interpreted as the real motive behind it. Some commentators also noticed that the election day was set during the period of university exams and after a long holiday which could make voting inconvenient for a lot of Thais who have to return to vote in their constituencies.[[36]](#cite_note-37)

In March 2023, a group of hackers posted the personal data of 55 million Thais for sale online. The group called 9Near with a symbol resembling that of the Move Forward Party, also mentioned on their page: "Almost election, choose wisely."[[37]](#cite_note-38)

In May, ex-prime minister [Thaksin Shinawatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thaksin_Shinawatra "Thaksin Shinawatra") tweeted that he was ready to return to Thailand before July 2023 and "enter the legal process". He faced possible prison time from prior convictions.[[38]](#cite_note-39)

The Thai economy was still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, but it was still struggling with multiple issues, including high energy and electricity costs, the number of employers still fewer than before the pandemic, rising household debts, and falling income growth. Other economic issues such as minimum wage, farm subsidies, and welfare were considered top voting issues. Most political parties campaigned on subsidies and tax exemptions.[[39]](#cite_note-40)

A total of 67 political parties applied to participate in the elections by party list system, of which 49 party numbers are selected by lottery and then in order of the application period.[[40]](#cite_note-41)[[41]](#cite_note-42)
